newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Goldman Sachs sees strong Latin American growth.
newsitem.headline: Goldman Sachs sees strong Latin American growth.

text.p: The largest Latin American countries are heading for one of their strongest periods of growth in decades over the next two years, Goldman Sachs's managing director said Tuesday.

"The group of six major Latin American countries could easily experience GDP growth rates averaging five percent in both 1997 and 1998," Gerald Corrigan, managing director of Goldman Sachs & Co, said in a speech at a bankers' conference in Buenos Aires.
"To put this in perspective, we would have to go back in history more than 30 years to find a similar pattern of more or less synchronized growth in Latin America," he said.

Corrigan added that there was no reason why the Argentine economy cannot grow by five to six percent this year and next, and said Latin American growth did not appear to be face much of a threat from potential increases in U.S. interest rates.
"At this juncture ... it seems unlikely that the magnitude of any such interest rate pressures will be of major proportions," he said.

Corrigan praised Argentina's economic reforms in recent years as "nothing short of astonishing." But he stressed the need for countries like Argentina to maintain their new-found committment to policy discipline, "because a failure to maintain that discipline will surely give rise to a repeat of the painful experience of the 1980s."

He also praised the reforms in Argentina's banking sector over the two years since the country was lashed by the Mexican devaluation crisis. But he added that Argentine banks need to continue reducing bad loans and improve communications with the Central Bank.

"The highest priority for the future is to find the most effective way to reduce the overhang of bad loans in the banking system and to further strenghen the credit decision making process such that new loans are of sound quality," Corrigan said.
